Yes. The deadlift target being 4 sets understates the hinge, because the deadlift is only one of the hinges in your week.

**Hinge work across the week**

| Day | Exercise | Hard sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Friday | Romanian deadlift | 3 × 6–10 |
| Sunday | Deadlift | 4 (top set + 3 back-offs) |
| Sunday | Hip thrust | 3 × 8–12 |
| Monday | Kettlebell swing EMOM | 12 minutes of swings, optional |
| Tuesday | PT legs day | deadlifts some weeks, every other week |

That is 10 hard hinge sets on the lifting days, spread across two days, plus swings if you do them. The pattern is covered twice a week, which is what I aim for. Glutes are very well served: every hinge, plus the squat, both split squats and the PT day all hit them.

**The one thing to watch is the hamstrings**

They get 7 direct hard sets (deadlift and RDL) plus a secondary role in hip thrusts and split squats. That is a fair dose, but every bit of it comes from the hip hinge. Nothing in the program bends the knee under load, which is the other half of hamstring training. The old routine had the same gap, so this is not a loss, just a note.

I would leave it for now. The bodyweight and body-fat trend matters more than another leg accessory while the phase is maintenance, and Friday and Sunday are already at 65 minutes of their caps. If the block-end report shows hamstrings behind, or you feel the back of your legs are lagging the front, the fix would be a knee-flexion exercise at home: Nordic curl negatives off the bench or slider leg curls on the floor, 3 sets, slotted onto Friday after the RDL. That would earn a swap of the single-leg calf raise off Friday to keep the session inside its time, since calves are also on Wednesday.
